Introduction/AI-SDLC/Product ideation

Product ideation

In this guide, product ideation covers product discovery: understanding user needs and testing possible solutions before development. Use research and prototypes to decide which problem to solve, what to build and when to stop.

Product owners, designers, engineers and reviewers work together to agree the requirements. Record them in a product requirements document (PRD), with relevant interface designs, research findings and open questions.

The activities are recommendations and the examples are fictional. Confirm who can approve investment, agree scope and accept risk in your organisation.

Start with the loop’s purpose

Use the steps below to frame a thesis, test assumptions and record a decision. For the shared model and the relationship between the loops, read the AI-SDLC overview.

How product ideation works

Ideation starts with incomplete information. Its job is to reduce the uncertainties that could invalidate the opportunity, the user experience, the delivery approach or the expected value. AI can speed up research, drafting and prototyping; people decide which outcomes matter and which trade-offs are acceptable.

The Defence Product Playbook, jointly developed by MINDEF and DSTA, makes a similar case. It treats a requirement as a hypothesis until an operator has used it, and recommends a product approach where the problem keeps changing. Its three principles align with this loop: define real problems, structure the team right and test early. This guide draws on the playbook as a reference; confirm how its roles and forums apply locally.

Know when to enter or revisit ideation

Start when the user problem, expected value or proposed behaviour is uncertain. The playbook names three signals: the need keeps changing, the root cause is unclear, or nobody can yet show that the solution will have the intended effect. Return when research, incidents or delivery work challenge those assumptions. A well-understood defect can go directly to implementation with a clear issue and acceptance criteria; it need not restart discovery.

Bring observations of the current task, support or operational evidence, existing alternatives and known constraints. Nominate a person to gather evidence and identify who can authorise the next investment. The output is a decision with its evidence, scope and unresolved questions.

Frame establishes what needs to be learned; Test supplies evidence; Decide records the next investment. Keep the criteria for commitment visible, and retain the learning when the decision is to stop.

Think of the loop in three parts:

  • Inputs: problems, user needs, strategic priorities, operational evidence, new capabilities and constraints.
  • Learning work: research, challenge, specification, prototyping, testing, measurement and synthesis.
  • Decision output: continue, change direction or stop, then update the product intent with what was learned.

Note

Agents can research and draft proposals. The product owner brings the evidence and a recommendation to the people authorised to decide on scope, investment and risk. Confirm those decision rights locally. Form the product and engineering team early, so that user value, feasibility, security and operational constraints shape the product before commitment.

Source: [2] “Why product ways of working” and “The three principles”.

Start with a thesis that can be disproved

A product thesis is a claim about why a product or capability should exist, written so that evidence could show it to be wrong. Without that property, each prototype tends to refine the idea rather than test it.

Recognise where the idea came from

An idea usually starts from a user or business problem, or from a new technical capability. Neither starting point is better, but each fails in its own way. Both need to arrive at an opportunity that is valuable, feasible and supported by evidence.

Two starting points for a product idea
Starting pointStrengthCommon failureQuestion to ask
Problem pull: a user or business problemAnchored in real demand and outcomesIncremental thinking that assumes today’s workflow must remainCould the problem be removed, rather than today’s solution improved?
Technology push: a new capability or lower costReveals options that were previously impossibleAn impressive capability searching for a valuable problemWhat meaningful problem is now feasible to solve for the first time?

Write the thesis

Record four things before exploring solutions:

  • User and problem: the target user, the task they are trying to complete, evidence that the problem matters and the consequence of doing nothing.
  • Outcome and value: the outcome the user needs, the value to the organisation and why the opportunity matters now.
  • Enablers, alternatives and boundaries: the enabling technology, current substitutes, other solution paths, and the assumptions, constraints, risks and dependencies.
  • Falsification criteria: evidence or limits, agreed in advance, that would trigger a redesign, a pivot or a stop.

Example · fictional thesis

A squad believes that service desk staff will resolve routine access requests faster with an assistant that drafts responses from the knowledge base. The thesis is weakened if staff cannot complete the task correctly, or if checking and correcting drafts removes the expected time saving. The experiment below turns those concerns into a test and a decision rule.

Test the problem statement before the solution

The Defence Product Playbook traces most weak products to a weak problem statement. It suggests building the statement from six questions, the 6W: what goes wrong, where, when and how often, who feels it, why it happens and why it matters. Then check what you have written against four criteria, the 4C.

The 4C problem-statement check, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
CriterionWhat the statement shows
ClarityOne user group, the task they attempt, the friction, and how severe and frequent it is
ConsequenceThe quantified cost if the problem stays unsolved
CauseA theory of change: the causal chain and the step worth intervening at
ConfirmationEvidence that supports the identified cause

The playbook names four traps: an aspiration, a solution in disguise, an end-of-life notice and a vague pain. “Our system is reaching end of life and needs to be replaced” describes an age, not a problem. Rewrite it around the users and the task that the ageing system now fails.

When there are more problem statements than teams, score each one low, medium or high for severity, frequency and reach (SFR). Start with problems that score high on all three. A severe problem that affects a few users once a year is a weaker first investment than one that is severe, frequent and widespread.

Next step: for your current idea, write one sentence each for the user, the outcome and the assumption that would most damage the case if it were false. Then agree the evidence that would show it is false, and check the problem statement against the 4C.

Source: [2] “Define the problem, measure the value”.

Widen the options, then narrow with evidence

The Design Council’s Double Diamond separates widening the options from narrowing them. The first diamond explores and then defines the problem; the second develops possible solutions and then tests them at small scale, rejecting those that do not work.

How this maps to the loop: Discover and Define expand and narrow the problem during Frame; Develop and Deliver expand and test solution options during Test. The agreed decision owner makes the Decide choices using that evidence. The diamonds are another view of the same learning work, not a second mandatory sequence.

The first diamond covers the problem space: discover widens understanding, define narrows it to a chosen problem. The second covers the solution space: develop widens the options, deliver narrows them through testing. The blue points mark decisions in this guide’s adaptation. The Design Council describes the four activities; it does not assign these decisions to an EDS role.

The Defence Product Playbook uses the same lens. It places problem definition in the first diamond and testing in the second, where testing has the greatest effect.

Use AI differently when widening and narrowing

  • When widening, use AI to research broadly, summarise evidence, generate different concepts, surface hidden assumptions and explore alternative journeys or technical approaches.
  • When narrowing, compare options against user value, strength of evidence, feasibility, cost, risk and strategic fit. Do not choose an option because it is the most polished or the easiest to generate.

Keep source links beside research summaries and check them before using a claim. Treat generated personas, synthetic interviews and an agent’s critique as prompts for research, not observations of real users.

Challenge the proposal before refining it

AI can turn a stakeholder request into a polished specification quickly. That speed creates a risk: refining an idea nobody has challenged. Before commitment, ask a reviewer, or an agent instructed to act as a critic, to work through these questions:

  1. What evidence shows that the problem is important and severe enough?
  2. What happens if the organisation does nothing?
  3. Which users experience the problem, and which do not?
  4. Why this solution rather than a materially different one?
  5. Which assumption could invalidate the whole thesis?
  6. What is the cheapest credible experiment that could disprove it?
  7. Which requirements conflict, and what fails at much greater scale?

This challenge complements user research and domain expertise; it does not replace them. Regulated, safety-critical, legally consequential and highly specialised questions still need qualified human reviewers.

Next step: before the next refinement session, put the seven questions to someone who was not involved in shaping the idea. Record the answers the team cannot yet support with evidence.

Sources: [3]; [2] “Test early, iterate fast”.

Prototype the riskiest uncertainty

Choose a prototype by the uncertainty it needs to resolve. A sketch may be enough to test a journey; a working integration may be needed to test feasibility. AI can help produce either, but speed and visual polish do not establish useful evidence.

SVPG distinguishes four product risks: value, usability, feasibility and business viability. Use these as prompts to check what remains untested. A usable interface does not show that people need it, or that the organisation can afford and operate it.

Choose the prototype by the question it needs to answer
UncertaintyQuestionSuitable prototypes
Opportunity and valueIs this worth solving?Concept prototype; business value prototype
Experience and adoptionCan people understand, access and use it?User experience, interface and content, or device and access prototypes
Feasibility and deliveryCan we build, connect and operate it?Technical or AI spike; functional prototype; operational or service prototype
Proof and readinessDoes it create value and operate safely at the intended scale?Proof-of-value pilot; production-shaped prototype

Prototype the riskiest assumption first. Give every prototype success criteria, an owner, and an expiry date or a decision on whether to promote it.

A prototype is not production code. Before any part of it reaches production, complete the architecture, security, testing, maintainability and operational reviews that apply, and version the validated artefacts against the user stories and criteria they support.

Next step: name the uncertainty you most need to resolve. Pick the row it belongs to and the simplest prototype in that row that could change the team’s mind.

Source: [4].

Validate, then decide

Validation is useful only when the method matches the question. Before testing, write down the assumption, choose representative participants or data, set a success threshold and name the decision the result will inform. Feedback then becomes evidence rather than opinion.

Write an experiment record

The following is a suggested working record. Complete it before testing so the result can inform a decision:

  1. State the assumption. Name the user, task and behaviour expected to change. Record the current outcome as a baseline.
  2. Choose the evidence. Record the method, participants or data, prototype version and conditions. Include relevant access needs and users likely to struggle.
  3. Set the decision rule. Agree a success measure, failure limits and a time or cost budget. Name the reviewer and next decision.
  4. Record observations and limits. Keep results linked to source notes. Separate what happened from the team’s interpretation, and record missing or contradictory evidence.

Example · fictional experiment

A service desk squad tests whether a draft-response assistant helps staff handle routine access requests. Eight staff complete comparable tasks using the current workflow and a prototype, with the order varied. The team records completion time, correctness, corrections and requests for help.

For this exploratory test, the team agrees to continue only if at least six participants complete the task correctly without help, the median time improves, and no response exposes restricted information. A mixed result triggers another targeted test. These invented thresholds guide the example; this small study does not establish a population-wide benefit.

Match the method to the question

Common validation methods and the evidence each produces
MethodQuestion it answersEvidence
Task-based usability testingCan users understand and complete the journey at the fidelity being tested?Usability, comprehension, task success
Proof of conceptCan the essential capability or critical workflow work?Feasibility, performance, limitations
Proof of valueDoes it create measurable value for a limited group in a realistic setting?Adoption, outcomes, business impact
Co-creation sessionWhat can users, product specialists and engineers discover and build together quickly?Ideas, prototypes, rapid feedback; confirm findings afterwards
A/B testingDoes a change to an existing product outperform a reliable baseline?Behaviour, conversion, performance

Ask participants to show how they complete the task, then use follow-up questions to understand difficulties. Report observed success separately from stated preference. For an A/B test, agree random allocation, a primary measure, sufficient sample size and a stopping rule before running it; a small convenience sample is not a reliable effect estimate.

Test with the people who will use it

The Defence Product Playbook groups fast learning into four habits, which it calls TEST:

  • Trial with real operators: test with the people who will use the product, not project team members standing in for them.
  • Expose the riskiest assumption: build the least you can to test the assumption most likely to sink the product, then discard it.
  • Shorten the loop: measure the time from user feedback to a changed prototype in days. If the loop is slow, fix that first.
  • Turn tests into decisions: end each test by keeping, changing or dropping the idea.

The playbook also gives reference points for pace: a proof of concept in front of real users within three to six months, and a proof of value with real users within a year. It presents these as prompts, not targets. If a team cannot reach them, ask what blocks it: access to users, procurement, funding or the team’s structure.

Fast iteration does not loosen assurance. Track resilience and security as guardrail measures alongside the value measure, and escalate any trade-off that carries real risk to the people authorised to accept it.

End every loop with an explicit decision

Review the evidence against the decision rule. When it supports implementation of a bounded scope, record a commitment decision and prepare the handoff. Otherwise choose one of the four responses below. If evidence is inconclusive, record that explicitly and identify the next test within the agreed budget.

Four responses when the team is not ready to commit
DecisionUse whenTypical next move
ImproveThe thesis is supported, but execution is underperforming.Tune usability, reliability, performance, cost or operating details.
RedesignThe problem is valid, but the current solution is weak.Explore a materially different solution.
PivotEvidence points to a different user, problem or value.Reframe the thesis and restart discovery.
StopThe thesis, cost, strategic fit or acceptable risk is not supported.Stop investing; keep the learning and any reusable assets.

A decision review can consider six dimensions: problem evidence, solution evidence, strategic fit, cost, risk and how the learning is trending. Agree limits on time, experiments or spending in advance. Stopping a weak thesis early is a successful learning outcome.

Keep reviews light and regular

Ideation needs enough structure to keep evidence moving without recreating heavy stage gates. A workable rhythm combines continuous agent work, frequent cross-functional evidence reviews and an explicit decision at the end of each meaningful learning cycle. At each evidence review, ask:

  1. What uncertainty did we address?
  2. What evidence changed our belief?
  3. What is now the highest-risk assumption?
  4. What decision is justified now that was not justified before?

Keep human approval where the consequences exceed the organisation’s risk tolerance. Examples include material regulatory interpretation, irreversible commitments to users, security exceptions, high-impact automated actions, costly architecture decisions and deployment into sensitive domains. Widen agent autonomy only when permissions, evaluation coverage, monitoring, known failure modes and rollback make the remaining risk acceptable.

Next step: at the end of your next prototype test, record whether to commit to a bounded scope, improve, redesign, pivot or stop. Link the evidence and any remaining uncertainty to that decision.

Source: [2] “Test early, iterate fast”.

Work as one product team with agents

Traditional product development often separates product definition, design, engineering and assurance through specialist handoffs. AI-SDLC favours continuous collaboration around a shared product intent, with each function working alongside agents in the same context.

Use the table to discuss responsibilities, not to assign formal authority. One person may cover several disciplines, but each decision still needs the relevant expertise and a named owner.

Illustrative division of judgement and agent-supported work; confirm roles locally
ParticipantHuman judgement and accountabilityAgent-supported work
ProductProblem, outcomes, priorities, trade-offs and thesisResearch summaries, options, draft specifications and decision evidence
DesignUser behaviour, desirability, usability and interaction principlesConcept variants, prototypes, journey analysis and heuristic checks
Engineering and architectureFeasibility, architecture, reversibility, security and operational qualityCode exploration, technical spikes, plans, tests and dependency analysis
AI and dataData quality, model behaviour, evaluation design and runtime controlsDataset analysis, evaluations, tracing and model comparison
Risk and compliancePolicy interpretation, thresholds, exceptions and accountable acceptanceContinuous checks, evidence collection, control mapping and risk screening
AgentsNo organisational accountabilityResearch, challenge, specification drafting, prototyping, testing and evaluation

For this to work, the shared environment needs:

  • access to current, relevant product and technical context;
  • clear ownership, permissions and decision authority;
  • visible agent activity, sources, outputs and status;
  • a structured route for review, feedback and exceptions; and
  • explicit human approval for high-consequence decisions.

Delegating work does not delegate accountability. The exchange also runs both ways: technical feasibility should shape ideas early, and user and business intent should shape architecture early. Doing both reduces late surprises about security, data location, performance, model limitations and operations.

Next step: invite an engineer and, where relevant, a security or data specialist to your next ideation review. Read about human–agent team composition.

Source: [2] “Structure the team right”.

Keep product intent connected

Product intent is the reasoning behind a product: why it exists, what it does, and the limits it works within. In many teams that reasoning is scattered across separate tools for evidence, requirements, design, architecture, policies and success measures. Missing or contradictory context can lead agents to make unsupported assumptions. Keep the sources, decisions and unresolved questions accessible together.

Trace outcomes into required behaviour and enabling architecture. Policies constrain all three, and evaluation checks all three. Keep these reasons explicit:

  • a product behaviour exists because it supports a user and business outcome;
  • an architecture choice exists because it enables required behaviour under known constraints;
  • a policy control exists because it addresses a defined risk; and
  • an evaluation shows whether the intended behaviour and constraints are met.

Keep product intent versioned, owned, accessible and auditable. Where practical, make the most valuable parts machine-readable: API descriptions, schemas, policy rules, acceptance tests and evaluation datasets can be checked automatically, not only read.

Treat the specification as a living document

In AI-assisted development, the specification is both an instruction for generating work and a basis for checking it. GitHub’s Spec Kit describes a common pattern that moves from a specification to a technical plan, then to tasks and implementation. During ideation, the specification develops alongside the evidence:

  1. Product intent is drafted as a PRD.
  2. A prototype tests the riskiest part of it.
  3. The evidence revises the PRD.
  4. The loop repeats until a validated PRD is ready for handover.

A useful specification is explicit enough to expose ambiguity, testable through examples, acceptance tests or evaluations, versioned and linked to outcomes, clear about constraints, permissions, non-functional requirements, edge cases and exclusions, and open to revision when evidence changes the intent.

Balance the level of detail. Too little forces agents to guess critical intent; too much creates false certainty. Increase precision as uncertainty is retired. Read about spec-driven development.

Next step: pick one planned behaviour in your PRD. Trace it up to the user outcome it serves and down to the test or evaluation that will show it works; fill any missing link.

Source: [5].

Measure learning and outcomes, not activity

Faster generation creates value only when the team can turn output into evidence, and evidence into better decisions. Start collecting evidence at the prototype stage instead of waiting for production. The cycle is: build, observe, evaluate, learn, update the product intent, and build again.

Draw on several kinds of evidence

  • User evidence: interviews, usability studies, support cases and co-creation sessions.
  • Behavioural evidence: product analytics, controlled experiments, workflow completion and adoption.
  • Operational evidence: telemetry, reliability, latency, incidents, model traces and recovery.
  • Evaluation evidence: offline datasets, automated tests, agent evaluations, policy checks and calibrated model-based judges.
  • Cost evidence: experiment cost, delivery effort, inference cost and the human attention consumed.

Use AI summaries to find themes worth checking against the original feedback. A summary does not establish cause, and an evaluation score covers only the cases and criteria used. Read how to evaluate AI behaviour and check model-based judgements.

Link each result to its research notes, dataset or test run. Keep participant information in the appropriate controlled location and summarise only what the decision needs. When evidence conflicts, record the conflict rather than averaging it into a reassuring conclusion.

Define success before building

Features shipped, prototypes generated, prompts submitted and lines of AI-generated code measure activity. They do not show user impact or business value. Define measures at each of these layers:

Suggested measurement layers; set local measures and thresholds before testing
LayerWhat it answers
User outcomeDid the user achieve the outcome that makes the product worthwhile?
Business outcomeDid the product create the intended value for the organisation?
Product behaviourDid users adopt the behaviour that should drive the outcome?
Leading indicatorsAre early signals moving in the expected direction?
Learning speed and costHow quickly and affordably did a hypothesis become credible evidence and a decision?
GuardrailsDid quality, safety, reliability, cost, privacy and fairness stay within tolerance?

Choose a value measure to steer by

The Defence Product Playbook describes a ladder of four kinds of measure. Teams tend to count what is easy, such as logins, uptime or features shipped, but those inputs do not show whether the problem is shrinking. Aim for the third rung, the value measure.

The metric ladder, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
RungWhat it shows
1. Input measureActivity or system operation, such as usage or uptime
2. Leading indicatorAn early behaviour change that supports part of the theory of change
3. Value measureThe intended outcome of solving the problem; the measure the team steers by
4. Outcome measureThe effect the organisation ultimately seeks; too slow to guide weekly work

Confidence that the problem is being solved rises up the ladder, but so does the time it takes to see a change. The playbook recommends one value measure per problem that can move at least twice a year. You should be able to explain how improving it improves the outcome measure above it.

Reject a candidate measure if it can be gamed without improving the outcome, or if its link to the outcome rests on assumption. Also reject it if it measures what the system does rather than what changes for the user, or relies on self-reporting. Check the remaining candidates against SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

Weigh value against cost. The playbook’s value-cost ratio divides the outcome delivered by the annual cost, and its year-on-year change is the signal to track. When value plateaus, consider moving the product to maintenance and investing in a problem that can still move.

Measures worth considering include:

  • Time to validated learning: elapsed time from an explicit hypothesis to credible evidence and a decision.
  • Cost per experiment: the cost of producing credible learning, including compute and human review.
  • Human attention ratio: the share of team time spent on users, strategy, judgement, difficult exceptions and learning, rather than producing documents and coordinating.
  • Product guardrails: task success, correction and escalation rates, model errors, latency, reliability, cost, privacy and safety incidents, fairness where material, and user trust.

Next step: for your next experiment, write the hypothesis, its start date and the success threshold. Record the date of the resulting decision to measure time to validated learning.

Source: [2] “Define the problem, measure the value”.

Prepare the handoff

Record the experiment results, decision, bounded scope and remaining uncertainties in the product intent. Link each acceptance criterion to the evidence and relevant prototype state.

Then use the shared handoff package and readiness checks with the people planning implementation. Resolve contradictions or give remaining questions an owner before commitment.

Continue to implementation readiness.
